This frozen grammar corpus comes from [TC39 Test262](https://github.com/tc39/test262/tree/2e0a56762801e275a9fdf96dc49d90ba0cddcf63). Original copyrights and the upstream BSD license are preserved. `manifest.json` records the selection, exact revision, flags, features and every file's SHA-256 digest. `tools/freeze_lexical_corpus.py` reproduces the selection from that revision.

The 815 files include 545 parse-phase negatives. The complete RegExp literal directories and all 192 parse-phase negatives under `built-ins/RegExp` are included, alongside Number/BigInt/string/template/hashbang syntax. The selected feature metadata contains only published ECMAScript 2026 features. These are **syntax checks**, not runtime conformance tests. Assertions, `eval` and RegExp constructors inside fixtures are never executed.

`tests/test_lexical_test262.py` honors `onlyStrict`, `noStrict`, `raw` and `module`; ordinary tests run in both script and strict mode. Inventory and digest checks prevent silent fixture loss. Run `python -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_lexical_test262.py`.

`tools/check_regexp_reference.py` separately validates a deterministic bounded pattern corpus using Node 24.15.0 as a development oracle. Node is not a parser runtime dependency. Four documented probes reveal one Node grammar defect: it accepts nested same-name captures such as `(?<a>(?<a>x)|y)`. [ECMAScript 2026 §22.2.1.4, MightBothParticipate](https://tc39.es/ecma262/2026/#sec-mightbothparticipate) requires rejection: the outer capture and inner capture are not in separate alternatives of a containing disjunction. The validator follows the dated specification. The oracle script records those exact differences rather than weakening the validator to match the engine.
